source.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Out-of-Distribution Detection
source.authors: Ayush Karmacharya; Luke Luschwitz; Lucia Romero; Ya-Nan Niu; Joseph Campbell

record.tranche_reason: Uses top-k SAEs to extract features for an OOD-detection method, but does not test superposition, capacity competition, or the geometry or canonicality of SAE features.
record.gate_note: The paper reports OOD-detection benchmark results and SAE concept-agreement results. The benchmark results do not test the claim versions. Figure 6's concept-agreement comparison bears on SAE features as a related subject, but not on whether they are complete, stable, or canonical units; it is recorded under fits_no_version. The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition in its references but reports no result from that work.
record.test_reason: The study uses top-k SAEs on frozen vision classifiers (ViT-B/16, ResNet-50) as a tool for OOD detection and reports its own method's detection performance. Its concept-agreement analysis (Fig. 6) measures whether VLM-labelled SAE latents match ID vs OOD images. That is a related construct, not a test of superposition geometry, capacity competition, or SAE features being complete, stable or canonical units. Toy Models of Superposition is cited only as a reference.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SAEs on intermediate layers of frozen vision models give a state-of-the-art post-hoc OOD score (SAID). They also conclude that VLM-labelled SAE concepts are a diagnostic: ID inputs activate concepts more consistent with the image than OOD inputs do. They draw no conclusions about superposition or canonical SAE features.
record.recipe_differences: Applies top-k SAEs to intermediate activations of pretrained vision classifiers for OOD detection and concept analysis, rather than testing toy-model superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported OOD-detection performance varies with SAE sparsity k and latent dimension; the paper says performance improves from very small latent spaces and changes only marginally beyond 1024 dimensions, while the effect of k initially improves and saturates beyond 448.

fits_no_version.finding: Across ViT layers, ID images activate SAE concepts that a VLM judges more often consistent with the image than concepts activated by semantic- or covariate-shift OOD images. The gap is larger in later layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision classifiers, SAE latents labelled by a VLM align more with in-distribution inputs than with OOD inputs.

record.problems: The study does not test the claim versions. Its concept-agreement finding is limited to vision models and VLM judgments; the paper also notes that its evaluation is limited to vision domains and that training separate SAEs for intermediate layers is computationally costly.
record.rows_left_out: OOD benchmark comparisons in Tables 1 and 2, layer and hyperparameter ablations, and other SAID performance results were left out because they measure OOD detection performance rather than the claim versions. The study does not report separate numeric concept-agreement values in the text.

untested.parts: No toy models, feature overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transitions.
No test of capacity competition or importance-based allocation as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of non-capacity sources of polysemanticity.
No LLMs. SAEs are trained on vision models, and there is no analysis of feature spread across neurons or of SAE recovery of ground-truth sparse features.
No test of SAE feature completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicality. Latent-dimension ablations report only OOD AUROC.

record.verdict_notes: Sensitivity results (performance saturating beyond about 1024 latents and k of 448) concern OOD AUROC only, not feature stability, so they do not bear on V5. The paper asserts that top-k sparsity encourages monosemantic features but does not test this. No embedded instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, feature overlap and geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity or importance-based competition.
Whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The claim concerns LLMs; this study uses vision models and does not test feature distribution across neurons or SAE recovery as evidence in LLMs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Measured VLM-judged semantic agreement of activated SAE concepts with input images.
rows.measure: Concept agreement: fraction of activated concepts judged semantically consistent with the image.
rows.note: The text reports higher concept agreement for ID samples than for semantic-shift OOD samples across layers; exact plotted values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Concept agreement for ID vs semantic-shift OOD measures a diagnostic of OOD inputs, not a claim version. Value is figure-only. State 'observed' describes the paper's own ID>OOD trend, not any version, so cannot_determine with respect to the claim.
